script.title: Why Japan's great port began as a village

lines: Commodore Perry sailed a fleet of American warships toward Japan.
In the 1850s, Japan had little contact with foreigners.
Perry arrived just south of Yokohama and demanded that Japan open ports for trade.
The Tokugawa shogunate agreed and signed a treaty.
One port was meant to be the town of Kanagawa-juku.
It sat on the Tōkaidō, a highway linking Edo to Kyoto and Osaka.
The shogunate decided that was too close for comfort.
So it built the port across the inlet, in the fishing village of Yokohama.
You see, it's like letting a guest sleep in your shed, not your house.
Foreigners settled in Kannai, a district surrounded by a moat.
Soon Yokohama printed Japan's first English newspaper.
In 1865, it made Japan's first beer and ice cream.
In 1872, Japan's first railway ran from Yokohama to Tokyo.
A small fishing village had become a famous port city.
Its name means sideways sandbar, because that is how it looked from the sea.

claims.claim: Perry arrived near Yokohama demanding Japan open ports; the shogunate signed a treaty, but built the port in the fishing village of Yokohama because Kanagawa-juku was too close to the Tōkaidō; it opened in 1859.
Foreigners settled in the moated Kannai district; Japan firsts in Yokohama: English newspaper 1861, beer and ice cream 1865, railway 1872.
Yokohama's name came from a sandbar seen sideways from the sea.

cast.perry: a 59 year old American naval commodore with a stern square jaw, grey bushy sideburns, a dark navy double-breasted coat with gold buttons and a black bicorne hat, 1850s
cast.official: a 48 year old Japanese shogunate official with a shaved forehead and a black topknot, a grey-blue silk robe with stiff winged shoulders and a dark sash, 1850s
cast.fisher: a 22 year old Japanese fisherman with a sun-darkened face, a wide straw hat, a short faded indigo cotton jacket and bare brown legs, 1850s
cast.trader: a 33 year old European trader with slicked blond hair, a thin blond moustache, a bright green waistcoat, a white shirt and a dark blue frock coat, 1860s
